questions.question: Design a URL shortener service like bit.ly.
questions.title: Design a URL Shortener (bit.ly)
questions.direct_answer: Generate a unique short code per URL by **base62-encoding a distributed ID** (Snowflake or DB sequence). Store the mapping in a **relational database** sharded by short code, with **Redis cache-aside** for hot reads. Redirect path is read-only and CDN-cacheable; the write path validates and persists. Expect a **100:1 read-to-write ratio**, sub-**10 ms p99 redirect**, and design for hot-key bursts on viral links.

interviewer_intent.testing: Distributed ID generation, read-heavy caching strategy, sub-10ms redirect latency, hot-key handling, and analytics decoupling.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using random short codes without collision detection, or storing analytics inline with the redirect (which kills latency).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Justify base62 over hash truncation, explain Snowflake vs DB-counter trade-offs, decouple click analytics through Kafka, and call out hot-key amplification with a local cache layer.

sections.title: Framing the Problem and What Makes This Hard
sections.content:
A URL shortener looks deceptively simple — "hash a URL, store it, redirect." The hard parts only show up under load:

- **Read-to-write ratio is roughly 100:1** — every shortened URL is clicked many times. The system is dominated by the redirect path, not the write path.
- **Sub-10 ms p99 latency on the redirect** — a slow redirect compounds into every product that uses your service. Caching and CDN strategy matter more than the database.
- **Hot keys** — a viral link can hit hundreds of thousands of QPS on a single short code. A single Redis key can melt under that.
- **Short-code collisions and uniqueness** — random hashes collide; a bad scheme either rejects writes or hands out the same code twice.
- **Analytics without slowing the redirect** — every click should be counted, but counting can't be on the critical path.

The central design choice is: **how do we generate unique short codes at high write throughput without coordinating across nodes**, and **how do we serve reads at near-CDN latency** without making the database the bottleneck.

sections.title: Clarifying Questions I'd Ask First
sections.content:
Before designing, I'd confirm:

**Functional**
- **Custom aliases** — do users get to pick their own short code (`bit.ly/myparty`)?
- **Expiration** — do links expire (TTL)? Default never, or some configurable max?
- **Analytics** — click counts, geo, referrer, user agent, time bucket?
- **Authentication** — anonymous shortening allowed, or accounts required?
- **Link preview / safety** — do we screen URLs against malware/phishing lists?

**Non-functional**
- **Daily writes vs reads** — the read:write ratio drives the architecture.
- **Latency budget** — redirect SLO?
- **Code length** — 7 characters of base62 give us ~3.5 trillion codes; is that enough horizon?
- **Geographic distribution** — single region or multi-region?
- **Data retention** — keep deleted links in a tombstone table or hard-delete?

sections.title: Assumptions I'm Locking In
sections.content:
For this design I'll assume:

- **100M new URLs/month** → ~40 writes/sec average, peak ~400/sec.
- **10B redirects/month** (100:1 read:write ratio) → ~4,000 reads/sec average, peak ~40,000/sec.
- **5-year horizon** → 6B total URLs, ~3 TB primary storage at ~500 bytes/row.
- **7-character base62 short codes** → 62^7 = 3.5 trillion code space, room for 500× growth.
- **Custom aliases supported** but rare (< 5% of writes).
- **Click analytics** — record every click, but asynchronously through Kafka, not inline.
- **Sub-10 ms p99** for the GET redirect; sub-100 ms p99 for the POST shorten.
- **Single primary region with read replicas + CDN edge caches** for global reads.

sections.title: Back-of-Envelope Capacity Estimate
sections.content:
**Throughput**

- Write QPS: 100M/month ÷ (30 × 86,400) ≈ **40/sec average, ~400/sec peak**.
- Read QPS: 10B/month ≈ **4,000/sec average, ~40,000/sec peak**.
- The system is **read-dominated by ~100×** — architectural bias goes to the read path.

**Storage**

- Per row: short_code (8 bytes) + long_url (~400 bytes) + user_id (8) + created_at (8) + click_count (8) + flags ≈ **~500 bytes/row**.
- 5 years × 100M/month ≈ **6B rows ≈ 3 TB** primary storage. Well within a single sharded DB cluster.
- Analytics events: 10B clicks/month, much wider rows (~1 KB) → ~120 TB/year → needs columnar store (ClickHouse/BigQuery), not the OLTP DB.

**Cache memory**

- 80/20 rule: 20% of links serve 80% of clicks → cache the **top ~10M short codes** → ~5 GB Redis (compact format), trivially fits.

**Bandwidth**

- 4,000 reads/sec × ~600 byte response ≈ **~2.4 MB/sec egress**, ~20 MB/sec at peak. Negligible.

**Conclusion:** read path needs a Redis cache + CDN; write path is small enough for a single primary with replicas. Real complexity is in the analytics pipeline.

sections.title: API Contract
sections.content:
Three endpoints carry the entire product:

```http
POST /api/v1/urls
Authorization: Bearer {token}
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "long_url": "https://example.com/very/long/article?utm=...",
  "custom_alias": "myparty",
  "expires_at": "2026-12-31T23:59:59Z"
}

201 Created
{
  "short_url": "https://sho.rt/xK9p2L",
  "short_code": "xK9p2L",
  "long_url": "https://example.com/...",
  "created_at": "2026-04-21T10:00:00Z",
  "expires_at": "2026-12-31T23:59:59Z"
}
```

Redirect (the hot path):

```http
GET /:short_code

302 Found
Location: https://example.com/very/long/article?utm=...
Cache-Control: public, max-age=86400
```

Analytics lookup:

```http
GET /api/v1/urls/:short_code/stats

200 OK
{
  "total_clicks": 14528,
  "clicks_24h": 312,
  "top_countries": [{"country": "US", "clicks": 8421}, ...],
  "top_referrers": [{"referrer": "twitter.com", "clicks": 4102}, ...]
}
```

Delete and a few admin endpoints round it out (`DELETE /api/v1/urls/:short_code`, `PATCH` for renaming aliases on owned links).

sections.title: Data Model
sections.content:
Two stores, two responsibilities:

**Primary OLTP table** (PostgreSQL or MySQL, sharded by `short_code` hash):

| Column | Type | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `short_code` | VARCHAR(10) PRIMARY KEY | base62, 7 chars typical |
| `long_url` | TEXT NOT NULL | original URL |
| `user_id` | BIGINT | owner; nullable for anonymous |
| `created_at` | TIMESTAMPTZ | for retention/ordering |
| `expires_at` | TIMESTAMPTZ | nullable; partial index where not null |
| `click_count` | BIGINT DEFAULT 0 | denormalized counter; eventual consistency |
| `is_custom` | BOOLEAN DEFAULT false | distinguishes alias vs generated |
| `is_deleted` | BOOLEAN DEFAULT false | soft delete |

Indexes: PK on `short_code`, secondary on `(user_id, created_at)` for the user dashboard, partial index on `expires_at WHERE expires_at IS NOT NULL` for the expiration sweeper.

**Analytics events** (ClickHouse / BigQuery / S3 + Athena):

| Column | Type |
|---|---|
| `event_id` | UUID |
| `short_code` | VARCHAR(10) |
| `clicked_at` | TIMESTAMPTZ |
| `ip_country` | VARCHAR(2) |
| `referrer` | TEXT |
| `user_agent` | TEXT |
| `device_type` | VARCHAR(16) |

Written asynchronously from a Kafka topic. The OLTP table never sees individual click events.

Relationships:

```mermaid
erDiagram
    USERS ||--o{ URLS : owns
    URLS ||--o{ CLICK_EVENTS : generates
    URLS {
        string short_code PK
        string long_url
        bigint user_id FK
        timestamp created_at
        timestamp expires_at
        bigint click_count
    }
    USERS {
        bigint user_id PK
        string email
        timestamp created_at
    }
    CLICK_EVENTS {
        uuid event_id PK
        string short_code FK
        timestamp clicked_at
        string ip_country
        string referrer
    }
```

sections.title: High-Level Architecture
sections.content:
The write and read paths are very different shapes. Read path is fronted by a CDN; write path goes through validation and ID generation. ```mermaid flowchart TB User([User Browser]) CDN[CDN
edge cache] LB[Load Balancer] Redirect[Redirect Service
read-heavy] Shorten[Shorten Service
write path] IDGen[ID Generator
Snowflake] Cache[(Redis
cache-aside)] DB[(PostgreSQL
sharded primary)] Replica[(Read Replicas)] Kafka{{Kafka
click events}} Analytics[(ClickHouse
analytics)] User -->|GET /:code| CDN CDN -.miss.-> LB LB --> Redirect Redirect --> Cache Cache -.miss.-> Replica Redirect -->|fire & forget| Kafka Kafka --> Analytics User -->|POST /urls| LB LB --> Shorten Shorten --> IDGen Shorten --> DB DB -.replicate.-> Replica Shorten -->|warm| Cache classDef hot fill:#dbeafe,stroke:#3b82f6 classDef store fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#ef4444 classDef stream fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#f59e0b class Redirect,Shorten,IDGen hot class Cache,DB,Replica,Analytics store class Kafka stream ``` **Read path (hot):** browser → CDN edge → (on miss) LB → Redirect Service → Redis → (on miss) read replica → 302 back. Click event fired async to Kafka. **Write path:** browser → LB → Shorten Service → ID Generator → primary DB → warm cache → 201 back.

sections.title: Short-Code Generation — Algorithm Choice
sections.content:
Three approaches come up. The decision depends on whether collisions are tolerable and how much you want to depend on a central counter.

| Approach | How It Works | Collision Risk | Coordination | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Random base62** | Generate 7 random chars, check uniqueness | Low but nonzero — birthday-paradox grows over time | None | OK for small scale, breaks at ours |
| **Hash truncation** (MD5 of long URL → first 7 chars) | Deterministic; same URL → same code | Very real at billions of rows | None | Don't use — same URL submitted twice gives same code, no analytics separation |
| **Distributed ID + base62** | Snowflake ID → base62 encode | Zero by construction | Each ID generator is sequential within its node | Industry standard — Twitter, Discord, Bitly |

**Snowflake ID structure** (64-bit):

- 41 bits timestamp (millis since epoch) — lets us sort by creation time
- 10 bits machine ID (1024 possible nodes)
- 12 bits sequence (4096 IDs per node per ms)

A Snowflake ID is monotonically increasing within a node, globally unique without coordination, and base62-encodes to ~11 characters — we truncate the leading bits to land at 7 characters by combining with a per-node prefix or using a smaller bit allocation.

sections.title: Why Base62 and the Encoding Detail
LLD — Class Design of the Shorten and Redirect Paths
Storage Choice and Sharding Strategy
sections.content:
**Why a relational DB for the primary store**

- The data model is tiny and well-shaped (one wide row per code).
- ACID guarantees keep custom-alias reservation race-free (`INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` in PostgreSQL).
- Read replicas scale read throughput linearly.
- Sharding by `short_code` hash is straightforward.

**Sharding scheme**

- **Hash by `short_code`** — distributes hot keys across shards (assuming generated codes are uniformly distributed, which Snowflake-derived codes are).
- **N=16 shards initially** — each shard ~200 GB; can split to 32/64 later via consistent hashing.
- **All writes go to one primary per shard, reads go to in-region replicas** — fanout is at the application level.

**Why not DynamoDB?** It would work — KV is the access pattern. But: cost grows with read units even for cached traffic, and we already need a relational store for user accounts and ownership. One DB to operate is cheaper than two.

**Why not store URLs in cache only?** Cache is volatile. A cold start (Redis restart) without a durable backing store would 404 every link. Cache must be cache, not source of truth.

sections.title: Caching Strategy and Hot-Key Handling
sections.content:
**Cache-aside pattern** with Redis:

- On read: check Redis → on miss, query DB → populate Redis with TTL of 24 hours.
- On write: write DB, then write Redis (warm).
- On delete: write DB tombstone, then `DEL` from Redis.

**Why not write-through?** Write traffic is 100× smaller than read traffic; write-through wastes Redis writes for codes that may never be clicked.

**Hot-key amplification** — a viral link creates a single Redis key receiving 100,000 QPS. A single Redis node handles ~50,000 QPS for simple GETs, so this melts Redis.

Mitigation, in order of complexity:

- **Local in-process cache** (Caffeine, 1–5 second TTL) on each Redirect Service instance — absorbs the bulk of repeat hits in-process, never reaches Redis. Eventual consistency window: a deletion takes up to 5 seconds to propagate.
- **Read-through CDN** with `Cache-Control: public, max-age=86400` on the 302 response — the browser and intermediate caches cache the redirect itself, never even hitting our origin.
- **Hot-key sharding** — if a single key still gets too much traffic, partition the value across multiple Redis keys (`code:0`, `code:1`, ...) and pick randomly on read.

**Negative caching** — cache 404s briefly (60 sec) so a typo on a viral non-existent code doesn't hammer the DB.

sections.title: Failure Modes and Graceful Degradation
sections.content:
**Redis unavailable**

- Redirect service falls back to read replica directly.
- Latency increases from ~2 ms to ~10 ms but the system stays up.
- Per-instance Caffeine cache absorbs the bulk of the load.

**Primary DB unavailable**

- Reads continue from replicas (slightly stale is acceptable).
- Writes fail — return 503 from POST endpoint with `Retry-After`.
- Writes pile up in a Kafka retry topic for replay after recovery.

**ID generator (Snowflake) unavailable**

- Local fallback generator using machine ID + nano-time + sequence.
- Brief uniqueness risk if clocks skew — NTP synchronization mitigates.

**Kafka unavailable (analytics broken)**

- Click events buffer locally on the Redirect Service in a bounded queue.
- On overflow, drop with a metric — analytics is lossy by design at the edges.
- The redirect itself **never fails because of analytics**.

**Cold cache after Redis restart**

- First few minutes of traffic hits the DB hard; we pre-warm the top 100K codes from a daily snapshot job.
- DB connection pool is sized for the cold-start spike, not steady state.

sections.title: Observability and Security
sections.content:
**Metrics**

- `redirect.latency` (histogram, alert on p99 > 10 ms)
- `redirect.cache.hit_ratio` (alert on drop below 90%)
- `redirect.requests.total{outcome="hit|miss|404"}`
- `shorten.requests.total{result="created|alias_taken|invalid"}`
- `db.replication_lag_seconds` (alert on > 5 s)
- `kafka.publish.errors` (alert on sustained errors)

**Logging** — structured JSON; never log full long URLs (PII risk for user-tracking links).

**Security**

- **URL safety scan** — check long URL against a blocklist (Google Safe Browsing API) at write time; cache results for 24 hours.
- **Rate limit by IP** at the shorten endpoint to prevent spam (50/min per IP).
- **Authentication for analytics** and delete — only the owner can see stats or delete.
- **HTTPS only** for the redirect domain — critical because the redirect URL itself can be abused for phishing if served over HTTP.
- **Strip tracking parameters** from the long URL on display (UI shows the canonical destination).

sections.title: Trade-offs and What I'd Change at 10× Scale
sections.content:
**At 10× traffic (1 trillion redirects/year):**

- **Multi-region active-active** with regional primary DBs and a Kafka-based replication stream for cross-region URL synchronization.
- **Replace Redis with embedded RocksDB on each Redirect Service** for codes hotter than 1,000 QPS — eliminates the network hop entirely.
- **CDN partnership** (Cloudflare Workers / Fastly Compute) to serve the 302 redirect at the edge with no origin hit for cached codes.
- **Sharded ID generator** with one Snowflake node per region to avoid cross-region coordination.

**What I'd reconsider:**

- **Snowflake vs DB sequence with batching** — each app instance reserves a block of 1,000 IDs at startup, refills when low. Simpler operational model than running Snowflake nodes; works as long as ordering across nodes doesn't matter.
- **Hash-based sharding vs range-based** — hash spreads load uniformly but loses range scan ability; for an analytics-heavy product, range sharding by created-at can be valuable.

**What I rejected and why:**

- **MD5 truncation for codes** — deterministic, so the same long URL always shortens to the same code. Breaks analytics (can't tell two campaigns apart) and creates a key-collision attack vector.
- **Storing analytics inline** — every click incrementing a row in OLTP creates contention on viral links. Decoupling through Kafka was non-negotiable.
- **Globally unique short codes via central counter** — one counter is a SPOF and a bottleneck. Snowflake's per-node sequencing solves the same problem without coordination.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **100:1 read-to-write ratio drives the architecture** — the system is fundamentally a CDN-friendly read layer over a small write store.
- **Snowflake + base62** for short-code generation — zero coordination, no collisions, monotonically increasing.
- **Cache-aside Redis with 24h TTL + local Caffeine for hot keys** — the layered cache absorbs viral traffic without melting Redis.
- **Click analytics decoupled through Kafka** — the redirect never blocks on analytics; pipeline writes to ClickHouse asynchronously.
- **Sharded primary DB by short_code hash** — distributes hot keys; reads fan out to in-region replicas.
- **CDN with `Cache-Control: max-age=86400` on the 302 response** — most clicks never even reach origin.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Clarifying questions I'd ask first**

- Custom aliases — do users get to pick their own short code?
- Expiration — do links expire?
- What level of analytics — just clicks or geo/referrer/device?
- Authentication — anonymous shortening allowed?
- How long should the short code be — 7 characters of base62 give us about three and a half trillion codes

**Assumptions for this design**

I'll assume 100 million new URLs per month, 10 billion redirects per month — so a 100-to-1 read-to-write ratio — a 5-year horizon, 7-character short codes, and a sub-10-millisecond p99 on the redirect.

**Quick capacity check**

- Writes: about 40 per second average, 400 peak
- Reads: about 4,000 per second average, 40,000 peak
- Storage: 6 billion rows over 5 years at ~500 bytes each is roughly 3 terabytes — fits a sharded relational cluster easily
- The system is read-dominated by 100×, so the architecture biases toward the read path

**High-level shape**

- Write path: client → load balancer → Shorten Service → ID Generator (Snowflake) → primary DB → warm Redis
- Read path: client → CDN edge cache → (on miss) Redirect Service → Redis → (on miss) read replica → 302 response
- Click events: Redirect Service publishes to Kafka fire-and-forget; downstream consumer writes to ClickHouse for analytics
- The redirect path never blocks on the database in steady state because Redis absorbs the traffic

**Short-code generation — base62 of a Snowflake ID**

- Snowflake gives us a 64-bit ID combining timestamp, machine ID, and a sequence number — unique without coordination
- Base62-encoding gives URL-safe, human-typeable codes
- I rejected hash truncation because the same URL would always produce the same code — breaks analytics and creates collision attacks
- I rejected random codes because at billions of rows the birthday-paradox collision rate becomes unacceptable

**Data model — two stores, two responsibilities**

- OLTP (PostgreSQL or MySQL): short_code, long_url, owner, expiry, click counter — sharded by short_code hash
- Analytics store (ClickHouse): one row per click event — written from Kafka consumer, never from the redirect path
- Custom aliases use `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` so two simultaneous reservations don't both succeed

**LLD — keep responsibilities clean**

- `IdGenerator` interface (Snowflake in prod, deterministic counter in tests)
- `UrlRepository` interface (JDBC in prod, can swap for DynamoDB)
- `UrlCache` for Redis access
- `ClickEventPublisher` for fire-and-forget Kafka writes
- `ShortenService` and `RedirectService` orchestrate — controllers stay thin

**Caching — layered, with hot-key protection**

- Cache-aside Redis with 24-hour TTL
- Local Caffeine cache (1–5 second TTL) on each Redirect Service instance absorbs viral hot keys without hitting Redis
- CDN with `Cache-Control: public, max-age=86400` on the 302 response means most clicks never reach origin
- Negative caching for 404s (60 seconds) prevents typos on viral non-existent codes from hammering the DB

**Failure handling**

- Redis down: fall back to read replica; latency increases but service stays up
- Primary DB down: reads continue from replicas; writes fail with 503 + Retry-After
- Kafka down: click events buffer locally and drop on overflow — redirect never fails because of analytics
- Cold cache after Redis restart: pre-warm top 100K codes from a daily snapshot

**Production extras**

- URL safety scanning at write time against Google Safe Browsing
- Rate limit by IP on the shorten endpoint to prevent spam
- HTTPS-only redirect domain to prevent phishing abuse
- Owner-only access to analytics and delete

**At 10× scale**

- Multi-region active-active with regional primary DBs and Kafka cross-region replication
- Embedded RocksDB on each Redirect Service for the hottest codes — eliminates the Redis network hop
- CDN edge compute (Cloudflare Workers) to serve cached 302s without origin hit

**Recommendation**

**Snowflake-derived base62 short codes, sharded PostgreSQL primary, layered Redis + Caffeine + CDN cache, Kafka-decoupled click analytics into ClickHouse, and HTTPS-only redirects with safety scanning** — essentially the architecture Bitly and TinyURL run today.

followup_questions: How would you handle a viral link receiving 1 million QPS on a single short code — walk through the cache layers and where they would melt.
Compare Snowflake IDs vs a centralised database sequence for short-code generation — when would each be the right choice?
How would you implement custom aliases without a race when two users reserve the same alias simultaneously?
What changes if the requirement adds full per-user analytics on each click (clicker's country, device, referrer) at the same QPS?

seo.metaTitle: Design a URL Shortener (bit.ly) — System Design Interview
seo.metaDescription: Complete walkthrough of designing a URL shortener: requirements, capacity estimation, Snowflake + base62 ID generation, sharded PostgreSQL, layered Redis caching, hot-key handling, and Kafka-decoupled analytics.

familiarity_anchors: Redis or in-memory cache fronting the store
30 to 50 to 1 read-to-write ratio is typical
speakable_v2.standard_example: POST /shorten with a base-62 7-char key, GET /{key} returns 301
speakable_v2.hook: I'd anchor on numbers first — capacity decides almost every design choice that follows.

groups.heading: Functional
groups.text: Shorten long URLs to 7-character base-62 short keys. Redirect on GET. Custom alias and click analytics are optional.

groups.heading: Non-functional
groups.text: Sub-50 ms p99 redirect. Three nines availability. Links live at least one year. Each link is unguessable from another.

beats.text: 10 million new URLs per day means about 115 writes per second average and around 600 at peak. Reads are 50 to 1, so 30 K reads per second. Each row is roughly 500 bytes, so 1.8 GB per day raw and around 650 GB over a year.

items: POST /shorten — body carries the long URL and optional alias. Returns the short key.
GET /{key} — 301 redirect to the long URL.
GET /{key}/stats — click count and per-day breakdown.

beats.text: One main table keyed by short key — long URL plus owner. Audit columns hold created-at and expires-at. A separate counter table or Redis HINCRBY for click counts avoids contention on the main row.

Edge load balancer fronts a stateless redirect service. The redirect service reads from a Redis cache. On miss, it falls back to the primary store. Writes go through a separate write API that checks alias availability and persists.

The bottleneck is the read path under hot keys. With 30 K reads per second, a 95% cache hit ratio still leaves 1500 reads per second hitting the database. I'd shard the cache by key prefix and keep the store partitioned the same way so a hot prefix doesn't burn one node.
Sequential keys reuse a counter and save a round-trip but make every link guessable from the last. Base-62 random keys cost an extra uniqueness check but stay unguessable. I'd take the random keys.

speakable_v2.cap: Numbers picked the design — caches, sharding, and a key strategy that holds at the year-mark.
followup_handoff: How would you handle a viral link that breaks the cache shard?
What changes if links expire after 24 hours instead of a year?
Where would you decouple analytics so they don't add latency to the redirect path?
How do you size the cache memory footprint for the working set?
